Mr. Austen Chamberlain, interviewed by Reuter, confirmed the report that complete Anglo-French agreement had been reached regarding security. He refused to discuss the details.
He said the agreement would be embodied in a Note which France would send to Germany in reply to the latter's pact proposals.
The Note, which would go as the French reply, was couched in very courteous and friendly terms ought to lead to successful negotiations.
Mr. Chamberlain said that nothing in the agreement was likely to cause Poland any disquiet.

New York, June 8.
The announcement that M. Callaux will use the Morgan credit of $100,000,000 to the franc has led to speculative buying of francs which briskly rallied at the opening of the foreign exchange market to 4/81, compared with 4/651, the lowest figure last week.

Adelaide, June 8.
The Italian aviator Major
Pinedo Hus arrived here.
Major di Pinedo-luded at the outer hurbour amid the cheers of thousands of spectators. He was welcomed by the Premier of South Australia.
In an interview Major di Pinedo said that Italy was apprehensive with regard to the future development of aviation and desired to keep well to the forefront.

Berlin, June 8.—Twenty-six machines having completed the fourth lap of the round Germany flight, 38 including four babies started the fifth and last circuit of 600 miles. The flights hitherto show that none of the machines under 40 horsepower completed four circuits. Eight under 80 horsepower succeeded, the best being an Udet with a 50 horsepower Siemens engine, while 15 were successful in the maximum, 120 horsepower class. Reuter
Cannada is sweltering in shade temperatures of 95 to 102. Fuhrenheit.
Ottawa spent the hottest week-end on record.
There were four deaths from heatstroke in Montreal and seven elsewhere.
There was a severe hailstorm in Eastern Ontario.

The great heat wave which for a week past has made life almost unbearable, suddenly broke yesterday on the eastern senboard. The glass has fallen twenty-five degrees in a few hours in the Boston district while the sea-breeze and a dense sea fog struck New York sending the refugees in the parks from the heat scurrying homeward for protection against the cold. Fatalities from the heat wave and storms totalled about 350. Meanwhile the heat wave continues in the west and middle west.
The Greek Legation reports that the leaders of the revolt at Samos have been captured.

Martiul law has been declared on Samos Island. The landing of a naval brigade and of troops was well received by the inhabitants, apparently only a small proportion of whom have joined the insurgents. The Council of the League of Nations opened to-day. Mr. Austen Chamberlain urged economy by the health section whose expenditure was 1,000,000 francs in 1925 compared with 700,000 in 1924.
A protest by Abyssinia against inclusion among the special zones where the traffic in arms is prohibited was adjourned to the next session as the arms conference is dealing with the matter.
The Council decided to refer the subject to the next Assembly of the League in September.

The annual meeting of the German Colonial Society passed a resolution strongly protesting against "the theft" of Germany's colonies; demanding that the Government ask for their return; and requesting the Reichstag not to ratify the Anglo-German commercial treaty unless the anti-German regulations still enforced in British colonies are cancelled.
The general committee of the arms conference has adopted a proposal to extend the scope of the clause prohibiting the use of poisonous gases in warfare to include the use of bacteria.
A mishap to the huge airship "Los Angeles," besides making exciting reading, has pointed the moral in two important matters.
The fact that the ex-Zeppelin "Los Angeles" had to abandon yesterday's flight from Lakehurst to Minnesota half way owing to engine trouble, has furnished the
Secretary of the Navy, Mr. Curtis D. Wilbur, with the text of a statement on the "utter folly" of staking the national defence exclusively on the reliability of the petrol engine.
